question: What proportion of adults admitted with a tibial fracture have a documented compartment syndrome check at least hourly for the first 24 hours?
why: Missed compartment syndrome is a leading cause of limb loss and litigation. The 2025 BOAST asks for hourly documented checks. No audit of check frequency in corpus; neurovascular audits [1312][1270] measure one admission entry only.

standard.source: BOAST Diagnosis and Management of Compartment Syndrome of the Extremities (updated July 2025)
standard.wording: Patients at risk of ACS should be assessed hourly with documentation of findings (whether present or not), an interpretation of these findings and rationale for management.

pass: In the first 24 hours after admission (or after fixation if sooner), no gap longer than 75 minutes between documented compartment checks, each recording pain and passive stretch findings.
population: Adults (16+) admitted with a tibial shaft, tibial plateau or pilon fracture. Exclude transfers out within 6 hours and patients on palliative care.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible admissions over the last 4–6 months
data_source: Nursing observation or compartment charts (paper or EPR flowsheet), admission clerking, theatre system for fixation time.

question: What proportion of adults discharged within 48 hours of a tibial fracture (or its fixation) have documented advice on self-monitoring for compartment syndrome?
why: Many tibial fractures now go home early, inside the 48-hour risk window. NICE asks for self-monitoring advice. No audit in corpus.

standard.source: NICE NG37 rec 1.2.7 (2016, guideline updated 2022)
standard.wording: In people with fractures of the tibia, maintain awareness of compartment syndrome for 48 hours after injury or fixation by: regularly assessing and recording clinical symptoms and signs in hospital; considering continuous compartment pressure monitoring in hospital when clinical symptoms and signs cannot be readily identified (for example, because the person is unconscious or has a nerve block); advising people how to self‑monitor for symptoms of compartment syndrome, when they leave hospital.

pass: Written or documented verbal advice naming compartment syndrome symptoms and where to go, recorded in ED notes, discharge summary or leaflet log.
population: Adults (16+) with a tibial fracture discharged from ED, fracture clinic or ward within 48 hours of injury or fixation. Exclude transfers to another hospital.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 3 months
data_source: ED record and discharge summary (EPR); fracture clinic letters; leaflet issue box if present.

standard.wording: The use of regional anaesthesia in extremity trauma: should follow joint decision making involving the patient (where able), anaesthetist and surgeon and include documented consent. should have an agreed policy that includes responsibility for post operative monitoring for compartment syndrome.

why: Photographs stop repeated dressing removal and help orthoplastic planning. Open fracture audits focus on antibiotics and timing [1587][1375]; photography is not measured.

standard.source: BOAST Open Fractures (December 2017); NICE NG37 recs 1.3.5–1.3.6 (2016)
standard.wording: Photographs of open fracture wounds should be taken when they are first exposed for clinical care, before debridement and at other key stages of management. These should be kept in the patient’s records.

pass: At least one wound photograph, dated before the debridement start time, retrievable in the EPR or clinical photography system.
population: Adults (16+) with an open fracture of any site (long bone, hindfoot, midfoot, hand, wrist, forefoot). Exclude deaths before surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive cases over the last 6–12 months
data_source: Theatre system, EPR media tab or clinical photography app, ED notes.

change: Enable the trust secure photo app on ED devices, with 'open fracture photo uploaded' as a required box on the ED trauma or referral form.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 on cases since the change, same template.

evidence: [1200] Open fracture STAT antibiotic prescription: 15.4% → 51.7% (clerking proforma)
[1587] UK open lower limb fractures: documented orthoplastic plan 85.8% (single cycle)

question: What proportion of adult trauma-team patients admitted under orthopaedics have a documented tertiary survey within 24 hours of admission?
why: Missed injuries are found late when nobody re-examines head to toe. [1989] found 11% within 36 hours (no re-audit); [2851] is paediatric only.

standard.source: South-East Scotland Major Trauma Guidelines, Tertiary Survey (NHS Right Decision Service, v1.0, reviewed 04/01/2025); use your own network guideline if it differs
standard.wording: Within 24 hours of admission 'after the dust has settled'.

pass: A structured head-to-toe tertiary survey entry dated within 24 hours of admission (repeated when awake if conscious level was reduced).
population: Adults (16+) seen by the trauma team and admitted under orthopaedics. Exclude ICU admissions with the survey done by ICU (record separately).
sample: 40 consecutive admissions over the last 4–6 months
data_source: ED trauma call log or trauma registry list, EPR ward entries, tertiary survey proforma.

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Put a tertiary survey proforma in the EPR and make 'tertiary survey done' a checklist item on the morning trauma meeting list.
reaudit: Wk 13–14, next 40 admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at trauma governance. Embed the proforma and trauma-meeting check if it works.
evidence: [2851] Paediatric tertiary survey: 34% → 72% (coordinators enforce as a discharge prerequisite)
[1974] Polytrauma secondary survey: 50% → 87.5% (trauma booklet)

question: What proportion of adults admitted with a complex fracture have a written summary sent to their GP within 24 hours of admission?
why: NICE asks for an early plain-English summary to the GP, not just a discharge letter. No audit of this in corpus.

standard.source: NICE NG37 rec 1.3.3 (2016)
standard.wording: Produce a written summary, which gives the diagnosis, management plan and expected outcome, and: is aimed at and sent to the patient's GP within 24 hours of admission; includes a summary written in plain English that is understandable by patients, family members and carers; is readily available in the patient's records.

pass: A letter or electronic summary with diagnosis, plan and expected outcome sent to the GP within 24 hours of admission.
population: Adults (16+) admitted with a complex fracture (open fracture, pelvic/acetabular, pilon, or multiple fractures). Exclude hip fractures (separate NHFD pathway).
sample: 40 consecutive admissions over the last 6 months
data_source: EPR correspondence log (sent timestamps), admission records.
